document.title: C Coding Guidelines
document.p: C in this project should read like a well-edited specification: every name says what it is, every interface states who owns what, and the compiler and linters catch violations before a human does.

These rules apply to all project-owned C, whether written by people or by AI agents. Agents are the main audience: they imitate surrounding code, so every rule here is either enforced by a tool (see Enforcement) or demonstrated in a golden file. A rule that is neither will drift.
When a rule and readability conflict, readability wins, but the exception is written down next to the code.

section.title: Naming
section.p: Spell identifiers out. We are not saving characters; we are saving the reader's time.

item.p: Case: snake_case for functions, variables, fields and types; UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for macros and enum constants.
Prefix: every exported symbol starts with sxml_, then the module: sxml_tree_append_child.
Functions are verb phrases: sxml_reader_read_line, not sxml_rdln. Predicates read as questions: sxml_node_is_element.
Types are noun phrases: sxml_parser, sxml_parser_configuration. Use no _t suffix, which POSIX reserves.
Variables say what they hold, including units: , , timeout_milliseconds, not n, len, t.
Loop indices are named after what they index: , not i. A loop over a plain counter may use index.
Booleans are named as true statements: has_namespace, is_empty.

section.p: Glossary. Each domain term has exactly one spelling, listed in docs/GLOSSARY.md. New terms are added (tools/spec/spec add term) before they appear in code.
Banned abbreviations (non-exhaustive, enforced by lint): ctx, buf, len, str, ptr, tmp, cnt, idx, num, cfg, res, ret, val, msg, err as a variable name.
Allowed short forms are only those the field itself uses as words: , uri, id, io, xml, xdm, qname (only for the XML QName concept).

section.title: Function signatures
section.p: Every project-owned function and function-pointer type takes at most three parameters, counting state and outputs. A required external callback signature may exceed this, with the exception documented at the declaration.
Three parameters force each argument group to name a real concept. Common shapes:

item.p: owner, request, output — act on an object with a described request and produce a result.
memory or allocator, configuration, output — bring an object into existence (see Object lifecycle).
view, output — a pure transformation of borrowed input.

section.p: Group arguments into structs that express a domain concept and a lifetime: a byte view, a configuration, a request, a lookup key, a result. Never create a generic context bag just to stay under the limit, and never move call-local pointers into long-lived objects to shorten a signature.
Call grouped interfaces with designated initializers so every argument is named at the call site:

Inputs come before outputs. Outputs are the last parameter and are pointers the caller owns. A parameter that is intentionally both read and written is named for that role (cursor_state) and documented as in/out.
Prefer two narrow functions over one function with a mode flag. A bool is allowed only as a named struct field, never as a bare positional argument.

section.title: Ownership and lifetimes
section.p: Every pointer in an interface is either borrowed or owned, and the declaration says which.

item.p: Borrowed is the default. A function that receives a pointer may use it only for the duration of the call and must not free or store it.
Storing a pointer beyond the call is part of the contract and is documented: "index keeps a reference to string_table, which must outlive it."
Transfer of ownership is visible in the name: sxml_list_take_entry, sxml_buffer_release_bytes. A function that returns owned memory says so and names how to release it.
Library code never calls malloc or free directly. Memory comes from the caller or from an allocator interface.
Arenas for many small objects. When objects are created in bulk and die together, allocate them from an arena and refer to them by index rather than pointer, so their lifetime is the arena's.

section.p: On failure, a function leaves its outputs either untouched or explicitly reset, and the header states which.

section.title: Object lifecycle and caller-provided memory
section.p: Every object type supports two lifecycles: one where the caller provides the memory, and one where the library allocates it through an allocator. The caller-provided path is the primitive; the allocating path is a thin convenience built on it.

row.cell: Places the object in caller memory; finalize releases internal resources but never the memory itself
Allocates, then initializes; destroy finalizes, then frees through the same allocator

section.p: The names are never mixed: create is always matched by destroy, initialize by finalize.

Memory requirements are queried, not guessed. Each type has a requirements function that reports size and alignment for a given configuration. The result is deterministic, so callers may compute it once and cache it.
Rules for both paths:

item.p: initialize never allocates on its own. It checks that the memory is large enough and correctly aligned, and returns SXML_STATUS_INSUFFICIENT_MEMORY or SXML_STATUS_MISALIGNED_MEMORY otherwise.

Growth is explicit in the configuration. An object that needs memory after initialization either receives an allocator in its configuration or works within a fixed capacity and reports SXML_STATUS_CAPACITY_EXCEEDED.
Objects do not move. After initialize, the memory stays at the same address until finalize. A type that is safe to copy byte-for-byte says so.
Composite objects compose requirements, rounded up for alignment, so a whole object graph can live in one caller-provided block.
destroy and finalize accept NULL and do nothing.
create stores its allocator inside the object so destroy needs no extra argument.
No fixed-size storage structs in public headers unless the size is deliberately frozen as part of the ABI.

section.title: Interfaces
section.p: An interface is a pair: a pointer to the implementation's state and a pointer to a constant table of operations. The library depends on interfaces wherever the host should be able to substitute behaviour: memory allocation, input and output streams, document resolution, clocks.

item.p: Operations tables are static const and shared by every instance. Per-instance data lives only in state.
Every operation takes state first and follows the three-parameter limit.
Interfaces are passed by value. They are two pointers.

p.strong: Lifetime is stated where the interface is accepted.

item.p: Calls go through small wrappers, such as sxml_allocator_allocate(allocator, request, &memory).
Every interface has a default implementation and a test double.
Interfaces are not extended in place. Publish a new interface type instead.

section.title: Errors
section.p: Fallible functions return an sxml_status enum; results go through the output parameter. Never signal errors through magic return values.

item.p: Status values are specific and named for the condition: SXML_STATUS_UNEXPECTED_END_OF_INPUT.
Ignored errors fail the build. Mark status-returning functions with the project's SXML_NODISCARD macro.
XPath, XQuery and XSLT dynamic errors carry their specification error code (for example FOAR0001) in an error record that the caller can inspect.
Detailed diagnostics go into an optional diagnostic record supplied by the caller, never into global state or errno.

p.strong: Library code never calls abort or exit, and never prints.
Every early return releases what the function acquired.

section.title: Memory and buffers
section.p: A pointer to data never travels without its length:

item.p: Units are in the name. and are different things.
Strings are UTF-8 byte views, not NUL-terminated, except at external boundaries.
Output buffers state capacity and bytes written, and what happens when capacity is too small.
Aliasing is declared; otherwise use restrict.
Untrusted input cannot cause unbounded work or memory. Limits such as maximum nesting depth are part of the configuration.

p.strong: No variable-length arrays and no alloca.

item.p: No recursion. No function calls itself, directly, through other functions, or through a function pointer or operations table. Walks over trees, expressions, types, patterns and nested values use a loop with an explicit stack or work list that lives in allocator memory and is bounded by a configured limit. Nesting depth in the input then costs heap, never C stack, so deep input cannot overflow the stack on any platform (WebAssembly has 64 KiB by default). Enforced by clang-tidy misc-no-recursion within a file; recursion through function pointers or across files is checked in review. Vendored third-party code is exempt ().
Size arithmetic is checked with checked-add and checked-multiply helpers.
One module, one header pair: include/sxml/tree.h and src/tree.c.
Opaque types by default. Expose fields only for plain value types such as views, configurations and requests.
Headers are self-contained and use #pragma once.
Internal declarations live in src/*_internal.h.
static for everything not exported; only the public API is exported.

section.title: Types and expressions
section.p: Target C17, with C23 features behind portability macros. Code must build with Clang, GCC, MSVC, the WASI SDK and the Android NDK.

item.p: Platform branches are few, each beside the existing _WIN32 one, and each says why in a comment. Android (, ): the NDK presets build for API level 24 (minSdk), where bionic lacks two C17 functions. src/allocator.c uses posix_memalign for aligned_alloc (API 28) and src/processor.c uses clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME) for timespec_get (API 29), both when __ANDROID_API__ is lower. Any other C17 function the library calls must be in bionic at API 24; tools/build-android.sh checks that by building all four ABIs with -Werror.
Integers: size_t for sizes and counts in memory, fixed-width types for values with a defined range, never plain int or long for data.
Distinct index types for distinct things (sxml_node_index, sxml_string_index) as single-field structs.
bool for truth values.
Enums for closed sets; switch on enums lists every case and has no default.
One declaration per line, at first use, initialized.

p.strong: Macros only for what functions cannot do.

item.p: No implicit conversions that change sign or lose precision.

section.title: Comments and documentation
section.p: Every public declaration has a contract comment covering what applies of: purpose, ownership of each pointer, units, aliasing, behaviour on failure, and thread safety.

item.p: Comments in implementations explain why, not what.
Cite the specification where behaviour follows it.
No commented-out code and no TODO without an issue reference.

section.title: Enforcement
section.p: Compiler, then linter, then structural search, then review. CI runs all of them.
Compiler flags (Clang and GCC): -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -Wconversion -Wsign-conversion -Wshadow -Wstrict-prototypes -Wmissing-prototypes -Wvla -Wswitch-enum -Wimplicit-fallthrough.
clang-tidy: see .clang-tidy.
ast-grep rules for banned abbreviations, malloc/free outside the allocator module, pointer parameters without a length, and bare bool parameters.
Runtime checks: AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer on every test run; fuzzing of every parser entry point.

Review rubric: names spelled out and in the glossary; at most three parameters with meaningful groups; ownership and units stated in the header; failure behaviour defined; no exception without a written reason.

item.p: Golden files. Every task names the golden module to match.
Headers first. Implementation tasks may not edit public headers.
Small, gated tasks with defined tests.
Separate review pass that reports findings without rewriting.
